rgod-01-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2016). Amun. World History Encyclopedia.
rgod-01-c1.quote: Amenhotep IV (1353-1336 BCE) succeeded his father as pharaoh
rgod-01-c1.claim: Amenhotep IV came to the throne of Egypt in about 1353 BCE, son of the long-reigning Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty.

rgod-01-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2016). Amun. World History Encyclopedia.
rgod-01-c1.quote: For the first five years of his reign Amenhotep IV followed the policies and practices of his father but then changed his name to Akhenaten
rgod-01-c1.claim: In about his fifth year the king changed his name to Akhenaten, usually translated "effective for the Aten",

rgod-01-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2014). Tutankhamun. World History Encyclopedia.
rgod-01-c1.quote: Akhetaten (`The Horizon of Aten', later known as Amarna)
rgod-01-c1.claim: He called it Akhetaten, "Horizon of the Aten", and the site is now known as Amarna.

rgod-01-c1.text: Barry Kemp (Amarna Project) (2026). Boundary Stelae. Amarna Project.
rgod-01-c1.quote: It was marked out by a series of tablets or stelae carved into the cliffs and escarpment on both sides.
rgod-01-c1.claim: Boundary stelae cut into the surrounding cliffs fix the city's limits and record his wish to be buried there.

rgod-01-c3.text: Joshua J. Mark (2014). Tutankhamun. World History Encyclopedia.
rgod-01-c3.quote: Tutankhaten came to the throne upon the death of his father in c. 1336 BCE at the age of eight or nine
rgod-01-c3.claim: Then a boy of about eight or nine took the throne as Tutankhaten, "living image of the Aten".
